newsitem.title: THAILAND: Religious unrest may spark Burma political tension.
newsitem.headline: Religious unrest may spark Burma political tension.

text.p: Although recent unrest among Buddhist monks in Burma's second city of Mandalay is religious in nature, there may also be an underlying element of political tension, diplomats said on Wednesday.

"The SLORC is concerned about security, especially ahead of Armed Forces Day on (March) 27th," one Rangoon-based diplomat said. "They are afraid the conflict between Buddhists and the Islamic community could evolve."
"Small things easily erupt into bigger things here," he told Reuters.

Burma's military government, the State Law and Order Restoration Council or SLORC, imposed a curfew and restrictions in several parts of Mandalay this week following monk demonstrations over the weekend.
Residents said on Wednesday an eight-hour curfew had been imposed from 8 p.m. and that several roads had been barricaded and the main market in downtown Mandalay was closed.

A government spokesman said the restrictions were imposed in order to maintain control. He told Reuters some elements in Burma were trying to promote misunderstanding between religions and eventually destabilise the country.
"The main reason for this tension...(is) to create unrest in the country by creating disturbances wherever and whenever opportunity arises," the spokesman said.

Diplomats said the new restrictions in Mandalay, the cultural centre of Burma and home to a large portion of the country's Buddhist monks, came because weekend clashes between the monks and Moslems turned violent.
At least two mosques were destroyed and several people were injured in attacks that appeared to be retaliation for the rape of a young Buddhist girl by a Moslem businessman, one diplomat said.
"My understanding is that there were riots on the (March) 15th and 16th. It seemed to be more of a socio-religious problem than a political protest," said another diplomat.
"From what we hear so far, it doesn't seem to have any political dimension at all, but this is a very repressed society; it is very volatile," he said.
Military control in Rangoon and other cities has been stepped up in recent weeks ahead of Armed Forces Day, when Burma's top military will all be in the capital.
Government officials said authorities fear terrorist attacks, especially by insurgent groups. Diplomats said they were also worried about uprisings by other groups.
Buddhist monks played a key role in pro-democracy uprisings that began in 1988, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the military regime.
At the time, top monks appeared on television to appeal for calm from the public and the military leaders.
The demonstrations were eventually quashed by the SLORC in a bloody crackdown that left thousands of people -- including monks -- dead or in jail.
Afterwards, monks continued to be involved in action against the military. Their protest tactics included a boycott on performing religious services for soldiers and their families.
Since then the Buddhist monks have been largely silenced, through fear and in part through offerings given to top monks by the generals in the SLORC.
But diplomats and analysts say there have been some signs recently of unrest among younger monks who want to see Burma return to democracy.
Opposition sources and diplomts say support from monks would be crucial for major change to take place in Burma.
"The young monks are like students. If they gather and talk together they could start something," a diplomat said.
The SLORC closed all major universities across the country in December after suppressing a series of rare student street demonstrations.
Analysts say they will likely be closed for several more months as the SLORC tries to diminish the possibility of further protests.
